newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street Wish List - Fed rate hike repellent.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street Wish List - Fed rate hike repellent.

text.p: If there were such a thing as a Wall Street wish list, it would include an all-purpose repellent to keep the stock market from getting stung by the interest-rate bug.

The interest-rate story was back in the news this week and stock investors were on the edge of their seats, waiting for next Tuesday's meeting of the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in March in a bid to ward off inflation.
The inflation bloodhounds have been sniffing for clues that the economy is growing at a pace that could put upward pressure on prices.
Another increase in short-term rates would drive up the cost of mortgages, home equity and other loans, as well as the cost of corporate borrowing.

The stock market has been on a roller coaster ride since March, when the Fed raised short-term rates a quarter point, to 5.5 percent, the first increase in more than two years. The central bank called the increase a "prudent step" to help prolong economic growth by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.
The move triggered a four-week freefall of 700 points in the Dow Jones industrial average between March and April, wiping nearly 10 percent from the world's most closely watched stock index.
The Dow lost 138.88 points to 7,194.67 Friday, but for the week it was up 25.14 points.

The uncertainty that the central bank may move again on Tuesday has shaken market confidence and brought tremendous volatility to stocks. Daily 100-point swings in the Dow have become so common that they no longer raise eyebrows.
By the end of the week, investors were still flipping coins on whether the Fed would pull the trigger on May 20.

What is making it tough for analysts to anticipate the Fed's move is that economic numbers do not seem to matter any more in the central bank's deliberations. The Fed is guided by its perception of inflation, making it difficult for most people to get a handle on what it will do.

The latest economic numbers released this past week confirmed again that inflation was not a threat. The Producer Price Index tumbled 0.6 percent in April, its biggest drop in nearly four years, while the Consumer Price Index rose just 0.1 percent.
The concern is that wage pressures will eventually spark inflation. But so far, few companies are complaining that salaries are creeping up to earnings-pinching levels.
The reason: productivity gains have offset higher wages.

The experts believe the interest-rate decision will hinge on the position taken by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, whose influence has grown at the central bank, where he is credited with slaying the inflation dragon.

But critics say the Fed, which has had problems explaining why the economy has been growing strongly without a hint of inflation for the last six years, may be looking at outmoded models from the 1960s, when hands-on workers were the main force in the economy.

The technology revolution has brought major bonuses, giving Corporate America the ability to cut costs and boost productivity. Nonetheless, Wall Street is still bracing for another tightening, possibly a quarter point rise in rates.
"If Greenspan decides that based on his economic philosophy that interest rates must go up, then they will rise," said John Geraghty at North American Equity Services, a consulting firm.

"Greenspan is a great believer of pre-emptive moves and he will select the statistics which back his argument that there's a threat of inflation, saying that the CPI or PPI are numbers that look back but rising commodity prices and the stock market are looking forward," he said.
"It's a case of selective economics," Geraghty said.
Larry Wachtel at Prudential Securities said the Fed will have a problem explaining another rate increase.

"The whole world will be ready to criticise them if they tighten again," he said. "My guess is that after this week's economic numbers, it will be so difficult for the Fed to explain a rate hike, that they will probably pass on it."
But others say the stock market is overly worried about interest rates.

"It's unimaginable that people can assume that a quarter point change in interest rates can affect a monstrous economy the size of the United States," said James Dines, author of the Dines Letter in Belvedere, Calif.
"It like a mosquito approaching an elephant with lust in its eyes," he said. "If you were a businessman, would a quarter point hike really matter?"
The one thing that is hard to escape, though, is that market psychology does turn bearish when there is threat of rising rates.

"It's the dogma of the day and it's politically correct to say that when interest rates are going to go up, it will raise the cost of doing business, and therefore is it bearish for the market," Dines said.

One often-overlooked fact is that the cost of borrowing is largely a non-issue for companies, since interest payments are tax-deductible. But much tighter monetary policy could become a problem for consumers, who have seen debt burdens soar, mostly on credit cards.
The Nasdaq Composite index slid 12.85 points to 1,340.73, for a gain of 5.68 on the week.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 12.13 points to 829.75 but was up 4.97 for the week. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.25 to 586.72, up 12.94 on the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks fell 5.21 to 432.44, but it rose 3.21 from last Friday.
